newsitem.title: UK: UK retail sales up in Oct but no sign of boom - BRC.
newsitem.headline: UK retail sales up in Oct but no sign of boom - BRC.

text.p: UK retail sales picked up pace in October after easing slightly in September, but there is no sign the 1980s consumer boom is about to return, the British Retail Consortium (BRC) said on Tuesday.
Its latest Retail Sales Monitor showed the annual increase in like-for-like value of sales accelerated to 5.9 percent from 5.2 percent in September.
This is someway below the very robust growth rates seen in the summer. In June, for example, like-for-like sales grew by 7.0 percent.

The BRC said the underlying rate of increase in the value of sales appeared to be steady at around 6.0 percent. "The growth appears to be stabilising at around that rate rather than accelerating further."
Andrew Higginson, chairman of the BRC economic affairs committee, said there was no sign of a runaway boom in spending.

"Whilst retailers are encouraged by this good performance there is no sign of the 1980 style boom that some commentators are talking up," he said. "The Chancellor should not risk damaging improving consumer confidence with any further interest rate rise."
Andrew Sentance, chief economic adviser to the BRC, said the effect on high street spending of last month's quarter-point rate rise remained to be seen.
"The fact that mortgage rates have not risen so far suggests that the impact will be slight," he said.
The BRC's findings for October were in contrast to the Confederation of British Industry's October survey which found sales soared to a eight-year high during the month.
The BRC said the survey was encouraging coming at the start of the run-up to Christmas. "The early indications of sales of Christmas specific items such as decorations and cards are encouraging."
The survey also found October was a particularly good month for clothing and furniture sales.
